newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lead down to 3.8 points in Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lead down to 3.8 points in Reuters poll.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole trailed President Bill Clinton by 3.8 percentage points in the Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll released on Saturday.
The poll of 1,200 likely voters was conducted by John Zogby Group International between Wednesday and Friday. It carried a statistical margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.
Clinton scored 42.4 percent in the survey, Dole had 38.6 percent, Reform Party candidate Ross Perot trailed with 8.4 percent and 9 percent were still undecided.
In the past 24 hours, Clinton's support rose by almost half a percentage point but Dole's grew by more than two points. Clinton's lead stood at 13 points just six days ago.

Other polls show Clinton with a more solid lead three days before the election. A CNN/USA Today Gallup poll on Saturday had Clinton 13 points ahead with 50 percent to 37 percent for Dole and 7 percent for Perot.
Pollster John Zogby said Republicans appeared to be rallying to Dole at the last minute while Clinton was suffering on the campaign finance issue.
"The president is taking a lot of hits in the media just as some of his soft supporters and undecided voters start to focus hard on their decision," he said.

In the past two weeks, it has been revealed the Democratic Party took in hundreds of thousands of dollars from Asian businessmen and the U.S. subsidiaries of Asian companies under questionable circumstances.
The party has had to return some of the money that was raised in violation of campaign finance rules.

Clinton on Friday insisted he and his party had "played by the rules" in collecting campaign money. But he called for changes in the laws that he said in the past were blocked by Dole, a 35-year veteran of Congress.

Top officials of the Democratic National Committee acknowledged in interviews published on Saturday in The Washington Post and The New York Times that under pressure to keep up with Republican fund-raising efforts they had not adequately scrutinized donors.
